questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Complementary Solution to a First-Order Inhomogeneous ODE
questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
{y}^{′}+6y=-5{x}^{2}+4x-7.
$$

Find the complementary solution ${y}_{c}(x)$ to this equation, where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the complementary solution, we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}+6{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Notice that this differential equation is separable since we can write it as

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{c}}{\text{d}x}=-6{y}_{c}.
$$

Therefore, we separate the variables as follows:

$$
\frac{1}{{y}_{c}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}{y}_{c}}{\text{d}x}=-6
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{y}_{c}}\,\frac{\text{d}{y}_{c}}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int -6\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{{y}_{c}}\,\text{d}{y}_{c} & =\int -6\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|{y}_{c}| & =-6x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we make ${y}_{c}$ the subject by exponentiating both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}|{y}_{c}| & ={e}^{-6x+C} \\  & ={e}^{-6x}{e}^{C} \\  & =K{e}^{-6x}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K={e}^{C}.$ 

Finally, we can drop the absolute value by allowing the arbitrary constant to be either positive or negative, i.e., setting $A=\pm K.$  Therefore, the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-6x},
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-4y=-4x-7.
$$

Find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.

${y}_{p}(x)=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $1.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $1,$ i.e.,

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha x+\beta 
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants to be determined. 

Calculating the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha .
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation:

$$
\alpha -4(\alpha x+\beta )=-4x-7
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
-4\alpha x+(\alpha -4\beta )=-4x-7.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}-4\alpha =-4\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,x) \\ \alpha -4\beta =-7\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =1,\,\beta =2.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=x+2.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y=-{x}^{2}-2x-2.
$$

Find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
questions.worked_solution:
The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $2.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $2,$ i.e.,

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha {x}^{2}+\beta x+\gamma 
$$

where $\alpha ,$ $\beta ,$ and $\gamma $ are constants to be determined. 

Calculating the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=2\alpha x+\beta .
$$

To find the values of $\alpha ,$ $\beta $ and $\gamma ,$ we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation:

$$
(2\alpha x+\beta )+(\alpha {x}^{2}+\beta x+\gamma )=-{x}^{2}-2x-2
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
\alpha {x}^{2}+(2\alpha +\beta )x+(\beta +\gamma )=-{x}^{2}-2x-2.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}\alpha =-1\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,{x}^{2}) \\ 2\alpha +\beta =-2\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,x) \\ \beta +\gamma =-2\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-1,\beta =0,\gamma =-2.$

Therefore, the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-{x}^{2}-2.
$$

2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y={x}^{2}-2.
$$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $2.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $2,$ i.e.,

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha {x}^{2}+\beta x+\gamma 
$$

where $\alpha ,$ $\beta ,$ and $\gamma $ are constants to be determined. 

Calculating the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=2\alpha x+\beta .
$$

To find the values of $\alpha ,$ $\beta $ and $\gamma ,$ we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation:

$$
2(2\alpha x+\beta )+2(\alpha {x}^{2}+\beta x+\gamma )={x}^{2}-2
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
2\alpha {x}^{2}+(4\alpha +2\beta )x+(2\beta +2\gamma )={x}^{2}-2.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}2\alpha =1\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,{x}^{2}) \\ 4\alpha +2\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,x) \\ 2\beta +2\gamma =-2\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =\frac{1}{2},\beta =-1,\gamma =0.$

Therefore, the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-x.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+5y=5x-4.
$$

Find the general solution to this equation given that the complementary solution is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-5x},$ where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

$y(x)=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{c}}{\text{d}x}+5{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-5x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $1.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $1,$ i.e.,

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha x+\beta 
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants to be determined. 

Calculating the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha .
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation:

$$
\alpha +5(\alpha x+\beta )=5x-4
$$

We then group the terms on the left-hand side, as follows:

$$
5\alpha x+(\alpha +5\beta )=5x-4
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}5\alpha =5\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,x) \\ \alpha +5\beta =-4\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =1,\,\beta =-1.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=x-1.
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{-5x}+x-1.
$$

$$

$$

To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

$$
2\frac{\text{d}{y}_{c}}{\text{d}x}-2{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $2.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular integral is also a polynomial of degree $2,$ i.e.,

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha {x}^{2}+\beta x+\gamma 
$$

where $\alpha ,$ $\beta $, and $\gamma $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=2\alpha x+\beta .
$$

To find the values of $\alpha ,$ $\beta ,$ and $\gamma ,$ we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation:

$$
2(2\alpha x+\beta )-2(\alpha {x}^{2}+\beta x+\gamma )=4{x}^{2}-4x+1
$$

We then group the terms on the left-hand side, as follows:

$$
-2\alpha {x}^{2}+(4\alpha -2\beta )x+(2\beta -2\gamma )=4{x}^{2}-4x+1
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}-2\alpha =4\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,{x}^{2}) \\ 4\alpha -2\beta =-4\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,x) \\ 2\beta -2\gamma =1\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-2,\beta =-2,\gamma =-\frac{5}{2}.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-2{x}^{2}-2x-\frac{5}{2}.
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by

$$
y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p}
$$

the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{x}-2{x}^{2}-2x-\frac{5}{2}.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Complementary Solution to a First-Order Inhomogeneous ODE
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
y' + y = -10.
$$

Find the complementary solution $y_c(x)$ to this equation.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the complementary solution, we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
y'_c + y_c = 0.
$$

Notice that this differential equation is separable since we can write it as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y_c}{\textrm{d}x} = -y_c.
$$

Therefore, we separate the variables as follows:

$$
\dfrac{1}{y_c} \cdot \dfrac {\textrm{d}y_c} {\textrm{d}x} = -1
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{y}_{c}}\,\frac{\text{d}{y}_{c}}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int -1\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{{y}_{c}}\,\text{d}{y}_{c} & =\int -1\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|{y}_{c}| & =-x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we make $y_c$ the subject by exponentiating both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}|{y}_{c}| & ={e}^{-x+C} \\  & ={e}^{-x}{e}^{C} \\  & =K{e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K= e^{C}.$ 

Finally, we can drop the absolute value by allowing the arbitrary constant to be either positive or negative, i.e., setting $A = \pm K.$  Therefore, the complementary solution is

$$
y_c = A e^{-x},
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

\frac{\textrm{d} y}{\textrm{d} x} +  y = x ^ 2 + 2x - 3.
$$

Find the particular solution $y_p(x)$ to this equation.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $2.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $2,$ i.e.,

$$
y_p(x)=\alpha x^2 + \beta x + \gamma
$$

where $\alpha,$ $\beta,$ and $\gamma$ are constants to be determined. 

Calculating the first derivative of $y_p$ gives

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}y_p}{\textrm{d}x} = 2\alpha x+\beta.
$$

To find the values of $\alpha,$ $\beta$ and $\gamma,$ we substitute $y_p$ and $y_p'$ into the differential equation:

$$
(2\alpha x+\beta) + (\alpha x^2 + \beta x + \gamma) = x ^ 2 + 2x - 3
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
\alpha x^2 + (2\alpha+ \beta)x + (\beta+ \gamma) = x ^ 2 + 2x - 3.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}\alpha =1\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,{x}^{2}) \\ 2\alpha +\beta =2\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,x) \\ \beta +\gamma =-3\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha=1, \beta=0, \gamma=-3.$

Therefore, the particular integral $y_p(x)$ is

$$
y_p(x) = x ^ 2 - 3.
$$
